public_rationale: Part of the claim holds. By early March 2026, the FT reported that Amazon's internal briefing note tied a 'trend of incidents' with a 'high blast radius' partly to 'Gen-AI assisted changes'. The note also listed GenAI usage without established safeguards as a contributing factor. Amazon itself admits that AI tools were involved in one retail outage and in a December AWS disruption. So problems linked to AI coding tools did show up in production. But Amazon publicly says only one recent outage involved AI tooling and none involved AI-written code. It calls the December AWS event limited and caused by user error. No independent source shows that the big outages, such as the six-hour one, were caused by AI tools. So 'big problems' from AI coding is only partly established.
limitations: The evidence centers on Amazon. Other industry incidents were not reviewed.
The internal documents are known only through FT and CNBC reporting.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Big problems from AI coding tools, such as AI-related outages at Amazon, have started to arrive as he predicted.

statement.excerpt: Right on cue, big problems have indeed started to arrive.
statement.document_title: “A spate of outages, including incidents tied to the use of AI coding tools”, right on schedule

from_speaker: big problems have indeed started to arrive
right on cue (following his warnings on GenAI code maintenance and coding-agent security)
FT: Amazon holds engineering meeting following AI-related outages
our_interpretation: Plain reading: by the post date (2026-03-10), significant real-world problems tied to AI coding tools had begun to show up in production. The Amazon outages reported by the FT are the example he gives.
'Big' is read as incidents with real customer or business impact, not minor glitches.
The claim needs AI coding tools to have been a real contributing factor. Being merely present during an incident is not enough.
criteria.support_condition: Credible reporting or company records show that, by early March 2026, AI coding tools contributed to significant production incidents, for example at Amazon.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evidence shows the reported incidents were not linked to AI coding tools, or that any AI-linked incidents were trivial.

evidence.excerpt: there had been a “trend of incidents” in recent months, characterized by a “high blast radius” and “Gen-AI assisted changes” among other factors
evidence.explanation: Amazon's own internal briefing note, as reported by the FT, tied a trend of high-impact incidents partly to GenAI-assisted changes.

evidence.excerpt: An internal document prepared for the meeting initially identified “GenAI-assisted changes” as a factor in a pattern of incidents stretching back to Q3.
evidence.explanation: Indicates that Amazon internally saw AI-assisted changes as a factor in a pattern of incidents over several months.

evidence.excerpt: Only one of the incidents involved AI-assisted tooling, which related to an engineer following inaccurate advice that an AI tool inferred from an outdated internal wiki, and none involved AI-written code.
evidence.explanation: Amazon says publicly that only one outage involved AI tooling and none involved AI-written code. This undercuts the idea of big AI-caused problems, though it concedes some AI involvement.

evidence.excerpt: Amazon acknowledged a limited disruption to a single service in one region last December but attributed it to a user error in configuring access controls, not a flaw in the AI tool itself.
evidence.explanation: An earlier AWS incident involved the Kiro AI agent. Amazon calls it limited and blames user error, which bears on how 'big' the AI-linked problems were.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: An independent or official post-mortem linking the major March 2026 Amazon outages, or other large incidents, to AI coding tools, or clearly ruling that link out.
